extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patentees, patent agents/attorneys, and persons preparing petitions/forms to Parliament or enrolments in Chancery; also printers/stationers
extracted.subtask_description: Forms, statutory provisions, and procedural requirements for obtaining, describing, enrolling, and defending letters patent (including notices/petitions to Parliament and Stationers' registration). Covers exclusivity language, assignment limits, specification/enrolment formalities, statutory limits on monopolies, and early copyright/printing registration rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive grant of sole use, exercise, and benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent grant to the named grantee (A. B.), his executors, administrators, or assigns the sole use, exercise, and benefit of the invention within the territorial scope specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form language: grant unto the said A. B., his executors, administrators, and assigns, the sole use, exercise, and benefit thereof; applied to England, Wales, Berwick-upon-Tweed, and colonies/plantations abroad when recited. Use explicit territorial and temporal language in the patent grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and corporate-activity limitation (no transfer to >5 persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent grant is subject to the condition that the grantee shall not transfer, assign, or profess to assign the liberty and privilege, nor open books for public subscription, nor receive sums of money from more than five persons, nor act as a corporate body, nor divide benefits into more than five shares; breach causes letters patent to cease and become void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proviso wording forbids transfers/assignments, public subscription, corporate actions, or dividing into >5 shares during continuance of the grant. If power/privilge becomes vested in more than five persons (including fiduciaries representing others), the letters patent shall utterly cease, determine, and become void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and enrolment requirement (instrument and Chancery enrolment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention and how it is to be performed in an instrument in writing under his hand and seal, and cause the same to be enrolled in the High Court of Chancery within the time specified after the date of the letters patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and proviso: failure to deliver a written, signed, sealed specification and enroll it in Chancery within the required period will render the letters patent and all liberties and advantages utterly void. The specification should state the nature of the invention and the manner of performance (i.e., the particulars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification content: describe invention 'in the words of the patent' and particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should describe the invention 'in the words of the patent' and then declare the nature of the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed, setting out the particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sample form begins 'Whereas ... by his letters patent ... gave and granted unto me ... my invention of [Here describe the invention in the words of the patent].' The compliance language in the form demonstrates the expected structure: recite patent, then provide the full particulars in a signed declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrolment/exemplification validity and favourable construction for grantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent, or the enrolment or exemplification thereof, shall be 'good, firm, valid, sufficient, and effectual in the law' and 'taken, construed, and adjudged in the most favourable and beneficial sense' for the advantage of the grantee, 'notwithstanding the not full and certain describing the nature or quality of the said invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form asserts that, despite imperfect description of nature or materials, the letters patent and their enrolment should be treated favorably for the patentee in courts and by officers—useful drafting principle though subject to later statutory and common-law limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of applying to Parliament: required contents for public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A public notice of intended application to Parliament must state the invention, identify the patents and their dates/terms/territorial reach, and describe the exclusive rights sought (including improvements and additions), so as to inform Parliament and the public of the bill's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of notice includes: invention title, recitals of letters patent obtained (dates and terms), territories (England, Wales, Berwick, Ireland, Scotland, colonies), and the exclusive right for the term of fourteen years. Notices often list improvements and the same particulars as appear in the patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to Parliament: required recital and prayer structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to the Commons should set out the inventor's expenditures and invention, recite the letters patent granted (dates, territories, terms), describe any improvements, and pray for leave to bring in a bill to prolong terms or vest exclusive privileges as the petitioner requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample petition language demonstrates the formal recital style (dates, territories, 14-year terms) and the concluding prayer asking for leave to introduce a bill to prolong the grants' terms and vest rights subject to parliamentary regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies declared void (general prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: All monopolies, commissions, grants, licences, charters, and letters patent made or to be made that amount to monopolies or dispense with law, or otherwise tend to erect or strengthen monopolies, are contrary to law and shall be utterly void and of none effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 21 James I c.3 opens by declaring prior and future monopolies and dispensations contrary to law, aiming to avoid grievance and inconvenience to subjects. This is a broad public-policy prohibition against monopolies in many forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies to be tried and determined by common law courts
rubrics_metrics.description: All monopolies and related grants ought to be examined, heard, tried, and determined by and according to the common laws of the realm (courts of King's Bench, Common Pleas, Exchequer), and not otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute mandates that the force and validity of monopolies be subject to common-law adjudication rather than Crown prerogative; practitioners should proceed in the common-law courts for relief or challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and penalties for those injured by monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons hindered, grieved, disturbed, or whose goods were seized by reason of a monopoly may recover three times the damages sustained and double costs; certain procedural protections restrict stays/delays and limit pleas like essoin or privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute prescribes treble damages and double costs, allows actions in common-law courts, forbids essoin, protection, wager of law, or more than one imparlance in such suits, and penalizes causing stays or delays of execution except by proper writs of error or attaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for previously made patents for new manufactures (up to 21 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act shall not extend to letters patent and grants of privilege for the sole working or making of any manner of new manufacture within the realm to the first and true inventor or inventors, previously made for one and twenty years or under; if originally made for more than 21 years, only 21 years shall be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This carve-out preserves older legitimate patents to original inventors up to 21 years. If an earlier grant had a longer term, only 21 years is to be recognized post-declaration; ensure term calculations reference the date of the first letters patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for future patents for new manufactures (14-year term)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the future, letters patent and grants of privilege for the sole working or making of any manner of new manufacture within the realm may be made to the true and first inventor for the term of fourteen years, provided such grants are not contrary to law or mischievous to the state by raising prices or hurting trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act explicitly allows limited-term patents for new manufactures (14 years from the date of the first letters patent), subject to public-interest restrictions. Draftsmen should ensure novelty and consider trade impacts to avoid contradicting the statute's provisos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and prerogative exemptions (printing, ordnance, alum, saltpetre, offices, charters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act does not extend to certain specific matters: existing letters patents concerning printing, commissions for saltpetre/powder/ordnance, certain offices then in execution, grants regarding alum mines, charters/customs of cities/corporations, and other specified prerogative matters—those remain in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple provisos preserve earlier grants or commissions of particular public importance (printing, ordnance, alum) or corporate rights. When assessing a grant's validity, check these statutory exemptions and historical survivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' sole printing rights under Statute of Anne (terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 8 Anne c.19 (Statute of Anne), from 10 April 1710: authors of books already printed who have not transferred rights, and booksellers/printers who have purchased copies, shall have the sole right of printing such books for twenty-one years; authors of books not yet printed shall have sole printing rights for fourteen years from first publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute creates statutory exclusive rights for authors/proprietors with specific term lengths (21 years for already printed works, 14 years for future publications). These are early copyright protections and set term and transfer considerations for printed works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for unauthorized printing and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who print, reprint, import, sell, or publish a protected book without the proprietor's consent forfeit the offending books and shall pay one penny for every sheet found in their custody; one moiety to the Crown and the other to any person who sues for the penalty; recovery in courts of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties include forfeiture (books to be turned into waste paper) and pecuniary fines; enforcement is in courts of record with actions of debt, bill, plaint, or information, and certain procedural bars (no wager of law, essoin, privilege, or more than one imparlance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration requirement in Stationers' Company before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: To be subject to the Act's forfeitures and penalties, the title to the copy must, before publication, be entered in the register book of the Company of Stationers in the usual manner; entries cost sixpence each and the register may be inspected at convenient times without fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration of a book's title in the Stationers' register before publication is necessary to secure statutory remedies against infringers; the register is to be kept at the company's hall, open to inspection, and entries/certificates involve fixed small fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerk of Stationers' duties and certificates (and penalty for refusal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The clerk of the Company of Stationers must register entries and, when required, give a certificate under his hand of such entry or entries (fee not exceeding sixpence). If the clerk refuses or neglects to register or certify when required by the author or proprietor, the statute provides consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical requirement: ensure the clerk makes the entry and issues a certificate as proof of registration; the clerk may take a small fee but must not refuse registration when properly presented.
